title: 2 Samuel 11:14–27
context: When the cover-up fails, David writes to Joab, sending the letter by Uriah’s own hand, ordering that Uriah be placed where the fighting is fiercest and then abandoned. Joab carries out the plan, and Uriah dies along with other soldiers. Joab’s message anticipates the king’s anger with a reference to Abimelech’s death at Thebez (Judges 9:50–54), and David replies with a cold proverb about the sword. Bathsheba mourns her husband, and afterward David brings her into his house. The section ends with the narrator’s verdict: what David had done displeased the LORD. Both traditions treat this verdict as shared ground: adultery and murder are sin against God, no matter who commits them, and God sees what is hidden.

verses.text: In the morning, David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
verses.arminianNotes:
The next morning David writes a letter to Joab and sends it by Uriah’s own hand. Uriah carries his own death sentence.

Arminian readers note that this is a cold and deliberate choice, made after a night to reflect, and that sin left unconfessed can move from adultery to murder when a person refuses to turn back.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the dreadful irony that Uriah’s faithfulness makes him the trusted courier of the order for his death, showing how far a believer can fall when he persists in hiding sin.

Both traditions read the letter as the moment David’s sin becomes murder, and neither tradition excuses him.

verses.text: He wrote in the letter, saying, “Send Uriah to the forefront of the hottest battle, and retreat from him, that he may be struck and die.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David writes that Uriah should be placed at the front of the fiercest battle and then abandoned so that he will be struck down and die. The order is explicit.

Arminian readers note that David uses his authority to make others complicit in his crime, and that the abuse of power multiplies sin by drawing others into it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the order is premeditated murder disguised as a casualty of war, and that the later judgment by Nathan names it plainly: David struck Uriah with the sword (12:9). God sees through the disguise.

Both traditions treat this verse as among the clearest descriptions of grave sin in the life of a believer in Scripture.

verses.text: When Joab kept watch on the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew that valiant men were.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab, watching the city, assigns Uriah to the place where he knows the strongest defenders are. Joab carries out the order.

Arminian readers note that Joab chooses to obey an unjust command, and that following orders does not remove personal responsibility for taking part in wrongdoing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Joab, already a man of violence (3:27), becomes complicit, and that sin in high places spreads through the people who carry it out, corrupting the community around the king.

Both traditions see Joab as morally responsible for his part, even though the guilt originates with David.

verses.text: The men of the city went out and fought with Joab. Some of the people fell, even of David’s servants; and Uriah the Hittite died also.
verses.arminianNotes:
The city’s men come out and fight, and some of David’s servants fall, including Uriah the Hittite. Others die along with him.

Arminian readers note that David’s sin costs other innocent lives, and that sin rarely harms only its intended target but spreads suffering to many.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator’s matter-of-fact report underlines the human cost of David’s plan, and that the deaths of other soldiers add weight to the guilt Nathan will later pronounce.

Both traditions see the loss of innocent soldiers as part of the grave consequences of David’s sin.

verses.text: Then Joab sent and told David all the things concerning the war;
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab sends David a full report on the war. The report will carry a hidden message.

Arminian readers note that Joab now holds knowledge of David’s crime, and that shared guilt binds people together in uneasy and dangerous ways, as later events between David and Joab suggest.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Joab’s report is a calculated piece of communication, and that the king who should be judging wrong is now dependent on the discretion of the man who carried out his crime.

Both traditions read the verse as a step in the narrative of concealment that God will soon expose.

verses.text: and he commanded the messenger, saying, “When you have finished telling all the things concerning the war to the king,
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab instructs the messenger to tell the king all about the battle. Joab prepares the messenger carefully.

Arminian readers note that Joab’s careful instructions show how sin requires management and cover, consuming the energy of everyone involved and drawing them deeper into deception.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Joab anticipates David’s reaction and frames the report so that the key information, Uriah’s death, comes last, an example of the calculation the cover-up now demands.

Both traditions see the instructions as revealing the moral cost of hiding sin, both for the king and for those who serve him.

verses.text: it shall be that, if the king’s wrath arise, and he asks you, ‘Why did you go so near to the city to fight? Didn’t you know that they would shoot from the wall?
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab tells the messenger that if the king becomes angry and asks why they went so near the city wall, knowing the defenders would shoot from it, the messenger should be ready. Joab expects a rebuke for poor tactics.

Arminian readers note that Joab knows the attack was tactically foolish, and that obeying David’s order required sacrificing sound judgment and soldiers’ lives.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Joab’s anticipation of royal anger highlights the hypocrisy of the situation: the king might rebuke tactics he himself demanded in secret.

Both traditions read Joab’s instructions as exposing how sin distorts leadership and judgment.

verses.text: Who struck Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Didn’t a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?’ then you shall say, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab expects David to cite Abimelech, killed by a woman who dropped a millstone from the wall at Thebez, and tells the messenger then to add that Uriah the Hittite is also dead. Jerubbesheth is another form of Jerubbaal, Gideon’s name.

Arminian readers note that Joab knows Uriah’s death will silence the king’s complaint, a grim sign that the general understands exactly what David wanted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the reference to Judges 9:50–54 recalls a ruler who died through his own reckless violence, a fitting and ominous echo for a king now acting violently.

Both traditions read Joab’s message as a coded confirmation of David’s crime.

verses.text: So the messenger went, and came and showed David all that Joab had sent him for.
verses.arminianNotes:
The messenger goes and tells David everything Joab sent him to say. The report reaches the king.

Arminian readers note that David receives the news he wanted, but the fulfillment of a sinful plan brings no true peace, and the narrative builds toward God’s verdict on what David has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the messenger is an unwitting participant in the cover-up, and that the chain of people touched by David’s sin keeps growing, showing how sin by those in power corrupts many.

Both traditions read the verse as a step toward the climax of the chapter in verse 27.

verses.text: The messenger said to David, “The men prevailed against us, and came out to us into the field; and we were on them even to the entrance of the gate.
verses.arminianNotes:
The messenger reports that the enemy came out against them in the field, and they drove them back to the city gate. He describes the action.

Arminian readers note that the messenger’s account is truthful as far as it goes, yet it serves a hidden purpose, illustrating how truth can be used to conceal a larger wrong.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the report presents the deaths as an ordinary misfortune of war, the very impression David wanted to create, while the narrator has already shown the reader what really happened.

Both traditions see the report as part of the disguise that God will expose through Nathan.

verses.text: The shooters shot at your servants from off the wall; and some of the king’s servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The messenger says archers shot from the wall, some of the king’s servants died, and Uriah the Hittite is also dead. The key news comes last.

Arminian readers note that Uriah is mentioned almost as an afterthought, yet to David it is the whole point, and the narrator lets the reader feel the moral weight of a man’s death reduced to a closing line.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the repeated phrase that Uriah is also dead echoes through the passage (11:17, 21, 24), keeping the victim before the reader even as the king tries to make him one casualty among many.

Both traditions honor Uriah’s memory and condemn the scheme that killed him.

verses.text: Then David said to the messenger, “Tell Joab, ‘Don’t let this thing displease you, for the sword devours one as well as another. Make your battle stronger against the city, and overthrow it.’ Encourage him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David tells the messenger to encourage Joab, saying not to let this thing displease him, since the sword devours one as well as another, and to press the attack. David answers with a proverb.

Arminian readers note that David’s words show a conscience hardening, treating murder as the ordinary chance of war, and warn how sin can numb moral sensitivity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the wordplay with verse 27: the Hebrew behind displease means be evil in someone’s eyes, so David says the thing should not seem evil to Joab, while the narrator will say it was evil in the LORD’s eyes. Many commentators highlight the contrast.

Both traditions see David’s coldness here as a measure of how far he had fallen.

verses.text: When Uriah’s wife heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she mourned for her husband.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Uriah’s wife hears that her husband is dead, she mourns for him. She is called Uriah’s wife, and Uriah her husband.

Arminian readers note that Bathsheba’s mourning is genuine and dignified, and that the narrator gives her grief space without accusing her, inviting compassion rather than suspicion.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the repeated naming of her as Uriah’s wife keeps the marriage before the reader and underlines the wrong David has done, an emphasis Nathan’s parable will take up.

Both traditions honor her mourning and recognize her as one who has suffered through David’s sin, not as a culprit.

verses.text: When the mourning was past, David sent and took her home to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
After the mourning, David brings her to his house, she becomes his wife and bears a son; but what David had done displeased the LORD. The narrator gives God’s verdict.

Arminian readers note that outwardly the matter seems settled, yet God sees all, and no concealment hides sin from him; this verdict is the turning point toward rebuke and the opportunity for repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the thing that David had done is named as his act alone, and that the LORD’s displeasure begins the work of judgment and restoration that follows in chapter 12, as God does not let his servant remain in hidden sin.

Both traditions treat this verse as shared ground: sin is evil in God’s sight, whoever commits it.
